ⓘ
How the SEC and TER sliders work. “Total float” is the number of working days a task can slip before it moves the launch date. Driving path = tasks with 0 or negative float (any slip hits launch). SEC sets the cut-off for the amber secondary band — tasks with float up to the number you pick (e.g. 5 d = “within 5 days of critical”). TER sets the blue tertiary band, a wider net (e.g. 10 d). Widen them to surface the near-misses that would join the driving path first if the schedule slips; tighten them to focus only on what’s already critical. They change what’s shown and coloured — never the schedule itself.

How to read this

The wave. Bars right of the red line are commitments. When a month's bar shrinks without the work completing, it reappears one or two months later — taller. Watch May 2026 empty into June–August.
The index. CEI has fallen every update: v4→v5 delivered 8 of 12 promised completions. A third of every month's plan now rolls forward.
Why it matters. A bow wave compounds: crews and facilities planned for a spread workload meet it all at once — right when TVAC and vibe need them.
A third of each month rolls forward. Who is actually delivering what they promise?

Which to believe

CPM is the floor. It believes the file — including the 12 durations that were cut without evidence. Treat 2026-11-02 as the best case.
Rate is the pattern. It ignores promises and projects what the team has actually done: 7.7% per month says late November.
Earned schedule is the discipline. SPI(t) of 0.79 prices in the execution record. If nothing changes, December 8.
Plan to the window, not a date: Nov 2 – Dec 8, 2026. September is no longer a defensible commitment.

Control · Margin & contingency

What buffer is left — and when it runs out.

Every margin activity is zeroed, the trusted solver re-runs, and the distance the target finish pulls in is the buffer actually protecting the date. Tracked across every status date, against the requirement line, with the erosion trend projected forward.

ⓘ
Three different things, three different names. Margin is a separately-planned buffer activity you manage on purpose (Schedule Management Handbook §5.5.11 — the handbook emphasises managing margin over float). Contingency is the calendar’s non-working time between the status date and the target. Float is a computed CPM quantity — the thing the handbook asks you to manage margin over. This page reports margin and contingency; float lives in Chapter 01.

Library · Weighted forecast

Segment by any field. Weight by the work left. Forecast the finish.

Pick a field and the tool splits the schedule by its values, recomputes BEI, CEI and SPI(t) for each segment’s own tasks, weights every segment by the work it still has to do, and blends them into a forecast for all work and for the project. A single project number hides who is really driving the date — this shows it.

ⓘ
How the forecast is built. Each segment gets its own performance factor (PF) from its SPI(t) — earned work over the work that should be done by now. Its remaining span is stretched by 1/PF to a segment forecast finish. Every segment is weighted by its remaining working days, because the future is where the remaining work is. The weighted all-work forecast blends them at the work-weighted composite PF; the project driving forecast is the latest segment, since the project can’t finish until its slowest part does. A segment with no completed work yet can’t form its own SPI(t) — so it inherits the project’s composite PF (capped at 1.0, the conservative EVM convention) and is flagged ◊ inherited. Its work is always forecast, never dropped.

Library · Your inputs

Beyond the schedule — the three things the file can’t tell you.

A schedule knows its own dates and logic, but not whether you have the people, the money, or the technical margin to hold them. Enter those three here and the tool folds each into a live Project-Vitals measure you can trend in the Metric Lab.

ⓘ
How this page works. Every field below is something you know and the schedule doesn’t. Pick the schedule version you are entering figures for, then type your current numbers — each panel spells out exactly what to enter, why it matters, and what the coloured readout is telling you. Each version keeps its own figures, so the whole Metric-Lab ribbon rebuilds from the numbers you enter here, version by version. Nothing you enter changes a scheduled date or calculation; it is layered alongside the schedule to expose risk the dates hide.

① Staffing coverage

you provide available heads · schedule provides demand
{{ bs.staffCov }}
COVERAGE
What to enter: the heads actually available to each team. Why: a plan you can’t staff slips regardless of logic. Tells you: where demand outruns supply — anything under 100% feeds directly into the bow wave.
IPT / TEAM REQUIRED AVAILABLE ✎ COVER {{ r.ipt }} {{ r.cov }}

② Funding alignment

you provide budget-to-go · schedule provides work-to-go
{{ bs.fundIdx }}
INDEX
What to enter: budget remaining per control account, as a fraction of its plan (0–1). Why: when money runs out before work does, the date is fiction. Tells you: which accounts are under-funded to finish — an index below 1.00 is short.
CONTROL ACCT BTG ✎ WTG IDX {{ r.ca }} {{ r.wtg }} {{ r.idx }}

③ Technical performance measures

you provide each margin and whether it is in tolerance · independent of the schedule
{{ bs.tpmPct }}
IN TOLERANCE
What to enter: each tracked engineering margin and a click for in-tolerance vs breach. Why: a green schedule hiding a red margin is the classic trap — a breach usually forces rework the dates haven’t booked. Tells you: the share of margins holding, so a technical problem surfaces before it becomes a schedule problem.
